newsitem.title: UK: UK manufacturing output to rise slightly in May.
newsitem.headline: UK manufacturing output to rise slightly in May.

text.p: British manufacturing production is forecast to show a slight increase in May but a drop could be just around the corner as sterling's appreciation starts to take its toll, analysts said.

A Reuters poll of economists showed a consensus forecast for manufacturing output growth of 0.2 percent month-on-month in May compared with 0.6 percent in April, and with the year-on-year rate forecast at 2.5 percent against 2.3 percent.
Overall industrial production, which includes output from both manufacturing and energy, is expected to grow 0.2 percent in the month and 1.1 percent year-on-year.
Both figures will be released at 0830 GMT on Monday.
"You feel the manufacturing sector is holding up quite well," said David Smith, chief economist at Williams de Broe.
But the growth holds a sting in the tail. "It increases the likelihood that the authorities will be fairly gung-ho on raising interest rates."

Many analysts felt Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget on Wednesday did not go far enough in reining in buoyant consumer demand and further rate increases are widely seen as inevitable.
Official interest rates are now 6.5 percent.
A rate rise would put further upward pressure on sterling, which has already risen around 18 percent since last August, and inflict serious damage on exporters.

Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, expected no change in industrial production and a slight improvement in the manufacturing figure, but he felt the outlook further ahead was not good following the budget.
"The budget relieved none of the upward pressure on interest rates, so although the latest data look OK, the outlook is deteriorating," Loynes said.
"I do not think the pound's rise has started to bite, but I am fairly gloomy about the long term prospects."
Smith said there was no question that the domestic economy was overheating but the strength of sterling was the main dilemma for the Bank of England in contemplating higher interest rates.
Peter Osler, economist for GNI, on the other hand, was comparatively upbeat about the outlook for the manufacturing sector for the rest of the year as a result of buoyant domestic demand.
"Interest rates have to be higher than the market is going for to slow down demand," he said.
"There is no way of not affecting the manufacturing sector by putting rates up, but we have had a cut in corporation tax which should help things along a bit".
Brown cut corporation tax by two percentage points to 31 percent, backdated to April 1997.
"We are going to see an improvement in manufacturing output as the year goes on, despite the pound hampering things, due to strong domestic demand," Osler added.
Some analysts said the large revision to the national accounts announced on June 27 made comparisons with former data very difficult.
"It is pretty near meaningless trying to forecast the figures...the data has been revised out of recognition," Smith said.
